area: Area X. Slow Flight, Stalls, and Spins
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain slow flight at commercial-pilot depth, fly it from the right seat within the CFI ACS tolerances while you talk it through, and teach it: set it up, demonstrate it, and spot and fix the errors learners make at the slow edge of the envelope.
why: Slow speeds are normal on every takeoff, departure, approach and landing, so slow flight is where a learner first meets degraded controls, big rudder demands and a small stall margin [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. Stall training builds on the skill learned here [[24:114|AFH 5-9]], and the FAA stall awareness work found that inadvertent stalls come from distraction during routine flight, not from practice stalls [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. As a CFI you will teach it early and revisit it often, so how you set the standard matters.

warmup: Think first: your learner is in level slow flight in the landing configuration, holding altitude well, 3 knots above the speed where the horn chirps. You ask for a 20 degree turn to the left. Before they move the yoke, predict three things that will change: what happens to the AOA, what the throttle must do, and which way the ball will try to go. Then ask yourself how you would let the learner discover each one instead of telling them.

key_terms.def: Flight at an airspeed where any further increase in AOA, increase in load factor or reduction in power would bring a stall warning [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].
The AOA where the airflow separates and the wing stalls. A given airplane stalls at the same AOA whatever its airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
The minimum drag speed. Above it, more power is needed to go faster; below it, more power is needed to go slower [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
Speeds between the minimum power required speed and the stall, where a lower airspeed needs a higher power setting to hold altitude [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].
The speed at the lowest point of the power required curve, where the least power holds level flight [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Below L/DMAX, a speed loss keeps growing unless the pilot reduces the AOA or adds power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
Lift divided by weight, in G. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].
At a high AOA the descending propeller blade takes a bigger bite than the rising one, moving the thrust center right and yawing the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
The spiraling slipstream that strikes the vertical fin and yaws the airplane; strongest at high power and low forward speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
The nose yawing away from the turn because the rising wing has more lift and drag; more pronounced at low airspeeds [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]].
The nose yawed directly into the relative wind with the ball centered, which the pilot achieves by actively correcting yaw effects [[24:113|AFH 5-8]].
Teaching each maneuver by outside references and flight instruments together from the first lesson [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

chunks.title: Slow flight today: purpose and the no-warning standard

body.p: Start with the definition, because the standard has changed. In slow flight any further increase in AOA, increase in load factor or reduction in power will bring a stall warning, such as buffet or a stall horn, and the pilot reacts to and corrects any stall indication [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. The AFH asks the learner to maneuver smoothly and coordinated without a stall warning, and to correct promptly if one occurs [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. The CFI ACS uses the same words: establish that airspeed (AI.X.A.S3), then fly straight and level, turns, climbs and descents without a stall warning (AI.X.A.S4).

Purpose (K1). Takeoff, departure, approach and landing are all flown at reduced airspeeds, close to the ground. Slow flight lets the learner meet that regime at a safe altitude and learn its feel, sound and visual cues: degraded control response and a harder time holding altitude [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. It is also the floor that stall training is built on: stall training covers the time from the stall warning to the stall [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

bullets: Element 1: slow to, maneuver at, and recover from an airspeed where the airplane is still controllable without activating the stall warning; 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed is a good target [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].
Element 2: fly it in the configurations used for takeoffs, climbs, descents, approaches and go-arounds [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

callout.text: AC 61-67C (2000) tells the instructor to have the student hold heading and altitude with the stall warning device activated [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a(2)]]. That is the older practice. Teach the current AFH and ACS standard: fly just above the warning, and treat any warning as a call to correct [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] (AI.X.A.S4).

body.p: Your briefing for this maneuver, and how private, commercial and CFI tolerances compare, are worked through in lesson AI.IV.A (Maneuver Lesson). Here the focus is the aerodynamics behind each element, flying it from the right seat, and finding and fixing errors.

callout.text: Application: say the definition in the learner's words before the first flight: 'We fly so slowly that one more bit of back pressure, bank or power reduction would set off the horn, and we never let it sound.' Then ask what each of the three triggers looks like in the airplane.

check.q: Your learner says, 'Slow flight means flying with the horn on.' How do you correct the idea, and what source backs you?
check.a: Slow flight is flown at a speed where any more AOA, load factor or power reduction would bring the warning, but without the warning; any warning is corrected promptly [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] (AI.X.A.S4).

chunks.title: Finding the target speed, entering and configuring

body.p: Pick the target in the configuration you will fly. The AFH gives a simple way: in the desired configuration slow to the stall warning, lower the nose slightly to stop it, add power to hold altitude, and note the airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. Introduce the maneuver with a target well enough above the stall for safe maneuvering but close enough to the warning to feel the low-speed characteristics [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

bullets: Clear the area, then reduce power gradually and raise the nose to hold altitude as the speed decays. Listen for the change in the sound of the airflow [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
Trim as the speed changes. If the airplane stays trimmed for cruise, strong back pressure is needed and precise control becomes difficult [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

Configure: slow flight is typically performed and evaluated in the landing configuration, using the before-landing checks, with gear and flaps extended only at speeds within their limits [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
Near the target speed, add power to hold altitude [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Below L/DMAX it takes more power to fly slower [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
Keep the ball centered with right rudder; the closer to the 1G stall, the more right rudder [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

body.p: Exit: add power; as airspeed and lift grow, use forward pressure to reduce the AOA and hold altitude; stay coordinated, level the wings as necessary and return to the desired flightpath. As speed increases, retract flaps and gear and retrim, expecting the AOA to change as they come up [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

Other configurations: clean or takeoff configuration is good training and may be evaluated [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. On the CFI checkride the aircraft is configured as specified by the evaluator (AI.X.A.S4). Note that the Task objective mentions slow flight in cruise configuration, while the skill element leaves the choice to the evaluator; prepare all of them.

callout.text: Abrupt or rough control movements in slow flight can cause a stall; abruptly raising the flaps is the AFH's example [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Teach flap retraction in steps as the speed builds.

check.q: How do you find this airplane's slow flight target speed in a configuration you have not flown before?
check.a: Slow to the stall warning in that configuration, lower the nose slightly until the warning stops, add power to hold altitude and note the airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

body.p: Angle of attack. AOA is the angle between the wing's chord and the relative wind. Past the critical AOA the airflow separates and the wing stalls, so the stall is the result of exceeding the critical AOA, not of too little airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. The critical AOA is roughly 16 to 20 degrees depending on the design, and a given airplane always stalls at the same AOA [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

Airspeed. As the airspeed decreases, the AOA must increase to keep enough lift for level flight; the lower the speed, the higher the AOA [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. That is why slow flight is high-AOA flight. Less airflow over the controls also means larger control movements for the same response, the 'mushy' feel [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

Load factor. Bank raises the load factor, and the stall speed rises with its square root [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. In a coordinated level 60 degree turn the load factor is 2G and the airplane stalls 41 percent above its 1G stall speed, because the pilot must raise the AOA to keep the extra lift [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. In a coordinated constant-altitude turn the load factor comes from weight plus centrifugal force [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

Before the first turn, ask the learner what the throttle must do; the AFH answer is more power [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

check.q: Why does a coordinated turn at constant altitude bring the stall warning closer even though the airspeed indicator has not moved?
check.a: The bank raises the load factor, so the stall speed rises with its square root [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]] and the pilot must increase the AOA to hold altitude [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

chunks.title: Power, the backside and the region of reversed command

body.p: Power setting is the part of K2 learners find least intuitive. Slow flight is flown well below L/DMAX, on the backside of the power curve. There, more power is needed to fly slower, so large power inputs or a reduction in AOA are needed to stop the airplane from decelerating [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

bullets: Region of normal command: at constant altitude, a higher airspeed needs more power and a lower one needs less. Most flying happens here [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].

Region of reversed command: below the speed for minimum power required (best endurance), a lower airspeed needs a higher power setting to hold altitude. It does not mean that reducing power makes the airplane slower [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].

Pitch and power: below L/DMAX small pitch changes cause large changes in induced drag and airspeed, so pitch becomes the more effective airspeed control and power controls the path [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
Speed instability: below L/DMAX, if turbulence knocks off some speed, the speed may keep decaying unless the pilot reduces the AOA or adds power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
Thrust helps hold the airplane up: in slow flight part of the thrust is directed upward and acts like lift [[1:99|PHAK 5-2]].

body.p: Where it bites. On a low-speed, high-pitch power approach for a short-field landing, power can reduce or stop an unacceptable sink rate; just lowering the nose without power gives a rapid sink [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. On a soft-field takeoff, climbing out of ground effect too early can leave the airplane unable to climb even at full power, and the only way out is to lower the pitch and accept some altitude loss [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

The elevator still has a role. On the backside, a little forward pressure makes a brief descent that lets the airplane accelerate toward the bottom of the curve, where there is excess power to climb or turn [[24:91|AFH 4-5]]. Throttle and elevator together manage the airplane's total energy; neither controls altitude or airspeed alone [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

callout.text: Application: demonstrate reversed command in two steps. Stabilize level at one slow speed and note the rpm, then slow 5 knots while holding altitude and let the learner see that the rpm needed went up. One demonstration is worth the whole graph.

check.q: A learner in level slow flight is losing airspeed after a bump and does nothing. Why does it not fix itself, and what are the two cures?
check.a: Below L/DMAX the airplane has speed instability, so the speed keeps decaying; the cures are reducing the AOA or adding power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

body.p: The rest of K2 lists what moves the speed at which the fixed critical AOA arrives. Teach each one with a sentence the learner can repeat:

More weight needs a higher AOA for the extra lift, so the stall speed rises

The stalling AOA is often reached at a higher airspeed, and more back force is needed

Less elevator is needed to reach a stall, so an inadvertent stall comes easier; the airplane is less controllable at slow speeds as the CG moves aft

Not a reliable stall cue: the wing can be stalled at any attitude and any pitch

body.p: The published 1G stall speed holds only in unaccelerated, coordinated flight at one weight and one CG, usually maximum gross weight and the forward limit [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Your learner's airplane on any given day may stall at a different indicated speed, which is one reason to find the slow flight target in flight rather than from the book [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

Altitude and temperature have little or no effect on the indicated stall speed; they raise the true airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]. Their real effect at the slow edge is on power, covered under environment.

callout.text: A light, forward-loaded dual lesson is not how the learner will fly solo or with passengers. Application: at least once, practice slow flight near maximum weight with the CG further aft (within limits) so the learner feels the lighter elevator forces the AC describes [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]].

check.q: Why can an aft CG within limits make an inadvertent stall in slow flight more likely?
check.a: As the CG moves aft, less elevator deflection and force are needed to reach the stalling AOA [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]], and the airplane becomes less controllable at slow speeds [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]].

body.p: Yaw effects close K2. In slow flight torque, slipstream effect and P-factor can produce a strong left yaw that needs right rudder, and the closer the airplane is to the 1G stall, the more right rudder it takes [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. At high power settings the yawing tendency increases further [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

body.p: Adverse yaw. When the ailerons roll the airplane, the rising wing gets more lift and drag, so the nose yaws away from the turn; rudder applied with the aileron cancels it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. Adverse yaw becomes more pronounced at low airspeeds, where larger aileron inputs are needed [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]] [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]].

Coordinated flight is the pilot actively correcting for these yaw effects so the nose points into the relative wind and the ball is centered [[24:113|AFH 5-8]]. The four elements vary from one phase of flight to another and between airplanes, so the pilot applies whatever control it takes [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

callout.text: AC 61-67C gives you two ready-made demonstrations at low airspeed: release the rudder and have the learner watch the left yaw, then have them enter left and right turns without using the rudder pedals to show adverse yaw [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a(6)]] [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a(7)]].

check.q: Your learner holds the ball centered in level slow flight, then adds power for a climb and the ball moves right. What happened and what is the fix?
check.a: More power at low speed and high AOA strengthens the left-turning tendencies, so the nose yaws left [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]; add right rudder to center the ball [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

chunks.title: Uncoordinated flight next to the stall

body.p: Uncoordinated flight (R3) is the risk that turns a slow flight mistake into a spin. A spin happens when a wing exceeds the critical AOA with sideslip or yaw at or beyond the stall. Yaw can come from wrong rudder use, adverse yaw from aileron, the engine and propeller effects, or wind shear and wake turbulence [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Mishandling the controls in turns, stalls and uncoordinated slow flight can spin even spin-resistant modern airplanes [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

bullets: Skid: ball to the outside of the turn; the pilot feels pushed toward the outside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
Slip: ball to the inside of the turn; the pilot feels pushed toward the inside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
A stall in a slipping or skidding turn can start a spin in the direction of the rudder applied, whichever wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
Keeping the nose from yawing before a stall recovery starts is the key to averting a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

body.p: Learners should develop a feel for slips and skids without relying on the instruments [[24:74|AFH 3-13]], but in slow flight the ball is your quickest way to see it from the right seat. Situations that hold uncoordinated control deflections are especially hazardous at low altitude, such as in the traffic pattern [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. That is the link to teach: the slow flight turn at altitude is the base to final turn at 600 feet.

callout.text: The spin avoidance part of a CFI applicant's own spin training is stalls and slow flight with realistic distractions, and it is unsatisfactory if the instructor must take control to prevent a fully developed spin [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300c]]. Coordination in slow flight is something you will be evaluated on, not just teach.

check.q: In a slow flight left turn the ball is out to the left, toward the inside, and the learner feels pushed inward. Name the condition and the spin risk.
check.a: A slip [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]; if the airplane stalls in a slipping turn it can enter a spin in the direction of the rudder applied [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

chunks.title: Stall warnings and inadvertent slow flight

body.p: Inadvertent slow flight and flight with a stall warning (R1). Real slow flight happens near the ground and often without the pilot noticing. Teach the setups by name:

bullets: Distraction: stalls from poor airspeed control are most likely when the pilot is busy with a checklist, a chart, a calculation or an item on the floor [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]].
Short-field power approach: a high sink rate in the region of reversed command needs power; lowering the nose alone gives a rapid sink [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Soft-field climb-out: leaving ground effect too early can trap the airplane where full power will not climb [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

Hot, high departure: in the AFH example the pilot keeps raising the nose over rising terrain, the airplane slows and stops climbing, and the stall horn sounds [[24:101|AFH 4-15]]. The way out is to give up some altitude to gain speed [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].

body.p: Flight with a stall warning is a loss-of-control precursor, not a place to stay. When the warning comes the response should be instinctive: add power, lower the nose and/or decrease the bank [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

callout.text: CFI ACS Appendix 3 (Tasks A and B): turbulence may cause a momentary stall warning. If you recognize it and promptly correct, that is not unsatisfactory; unsatisfactory is continual deviation, lack of correction or lack of recognition.

Application: compare the AFH's 5 to 10 knot target [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] with a horn that may sound up to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. In some airplanes the low end of the target will sound the horn. That is why the AFH method of finding the speed from the warning matters [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

check.q: Your learner's airplane has no stall horn, only buffet. What do you stress about the warning in slow flight?
check.a: Certification allows the warning to be pre-stall buffet rather than a device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]], so the learner must know the feel, sound and visual cues of slow flight [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] and correct at the first buffet.

body.p: Effect of environmental elements on airplane performance (R4). Teach each one by what it does to the slow flight margin:

bullets: Turbulence: a vertical gust or wind shear can suddenly change the relative wind and raise the AOA, so the airplane can stall at a significantly higher airspeed than in smooth air [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. In slow flight speed instability makes it worse: a gust that knocks off speed leaves it decaying [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

Microbursts: a downburst is dangerous in the climb after takeoff and on approach because the airplane is slow; a major wind change can cost lift and cause a crash [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. A pilot who reduced power and lowered the nose for the headwind shear is left nose-low and power-low for the tailwind shear, which can cause a stall or a landing short [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].

High density altitude: the indicated stall speed hardly changes [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]], but a higher density altitude reduces the engine's power output [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]]. Application: in slow flight, where power holds altitude below L/DMAX [[24:115|AFH 5-10]], there may be little or no power left to stop a sink or a deceleration.

body.p: Practice on a marginal day is itself an environmental risk. The AIH example is slow flight and stalls planned under marginal VFR: coach the learner to name the risks, such as entering IMC or practicing too low, and change the plan to the pattern, a simulation device or ground school, or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

callout.text: The AIH names teaching stalls below a cloud layer, which leaves too little altitude to recover, as an inappropriate altitude [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Slow flight carries the same risk, since an inadvertent stall is what you are guarding against (application).

Application: on a bumpy day, let the learner feel a gust push the airplane toward the horn at a fixed target speed. Then ask what they would do on short final in the same air. AC 61-67C says to carry a higher than normal approach speed in moderate to severe turbulence [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

check.q: Your practice area is hot and high. The indicated stall speed is about the same as at sea level, so what makes slow flight harder?
check.a: Higher density altitude reduces engine power [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]], and below L/DMAX it takes more power to fly slower [[24:115|AFH 5-10]], so there is less margin to hold altitude or recover.

body.p: Collision hazards (R5) and clearing the area (S1). The AIM asks training operators to have pilots call out 'clear' left, right, above or below, to raise the wing toward the turn and look in a high-wing airplane or lower it in a low-wing airplane, and to clear before all turns and maneuvers, slow flight included [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. Slow flight adds its own limits on the scan: the airplane's attitude creates extra blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]], and every climb, descent and turn in the maneuver is a new direction to clear. Teach a clearing procedure and insist on it before every maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

Entry altitude (S2). Plan so the maneuver can be completed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL in a single-engine airplane, or higher if the manufacturer recommends it, so there is room to recover from an inadvertent stall [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] (AI.X.A.S2). Use the highest terrain in the area and add the descents you plan to fly.
Distractions, task prioritization, loss of situational awareness or disorientation (R6):

bullets: Distractions: most stall/spin accidents came when the pilot's attention was diverted from flying; intentional practice seldom caused one [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Task prioritization: slow flight teaches dividing attention between aircraft control and other demands [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. Teach 'fly first': when the horn or the airspeed calls, the secondary task waits.

Loss of situational awareness: inability to divide attention between control and orientation, and fixation on the flight instruments, are both listed slow flight errors [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. A learner staring at the airspeed indicator drifts off heading, into traffic or out of the practice area.

Disorientation: integrated flight instruction teaches each maneuver by outside and instrument references together, so the learner keeps control if outside references are lost for a short time [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Learners who believe the instructor does all the scanning do not build the habit, and flight instructors were on board in 37 percent of the midair collisions in one study [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Make lookout a shared job [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: The highest terrain under your practice area is 1,800 feet MSL and you plan slow flight descents totaling 300 feet. What is the lowest entry altitude?
check.a: 1,800 + 1,500 + 300 = 3,600 feet MSL, so the maneuver ends no lower than 1,500 feet AGL [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] (AI.X.A.S2).

chunks.title: Fly it while you explain it

body.p: On the CFI checkride you demonstrate and explain at the same time. Explain power settings and attitudes as you fly, in the same order you briefed them, and if the demonstration does not match the explanation, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. A sample right-seat script (application, built from the AFH procedure):

bullets: 1. 'Clearing turns now: clear left, clear right, clear above and below.' Confirm the entry altitude allows completion no lower than 1,500 feet AGL [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] (S1, S2).
2. 'Power coming back; I raise the nose to hold altitude and trim as the speed falls. Hear the airflow change.' [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
3. 'Flaps and gear within their speed limits, before-landing check done.' [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] (S4, configuration as the evaluator specified).
4. 'Approaching the target: power up to hold altitude. Below L/DMAX it takes more power to fly slower.' [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] (S3).
5. 'Right rudder to keep the ball centered; feel how the controls are mushy and need bigger movements.' [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
6. 'Turning 20 degrees: more power to hold altitude, rudder with aileron for adverse yaw.' [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]] (S4).
7. 'Climbing and descending with power; pitch holds the airspeed.' [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] (S4).
8. 'Exit: power, forward pressure as the speed builds, coordinated, flaps up in steps, retrim.' [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]

Completed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ASEL)
S3 Airspeed chosen
Any further increase in AOA, increase in load factor, or reduction in power would result in a stall warning
S4 Maneuvers
Coordinated straight-and-level flight, turns, climbs and descents, configured as specified by the evaluator, without a stall warning
S5 Altitude
Specified altitude, ±50 feet
S5 Heading
Specified heading, ±10°
S5 Airspeed
+5/-0 knots
S5 Bank
Specified angle of bank, ±5°

body.p: The -0 on airspeed is the heart of the standard: any steady speed below the one you set is a step toward the warning. Talking while flying makes this harder, which is the point of the CFI version. The AFH notes that it is more difficult to hold a selected altitude in this regime [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

callout.text: Application: before each item, glance at the altimeter and airspeed, speak one sentence, then glance again. Long explanations belong on the ground; in the air, short sentences keep your scan alive.

check.q: During your demonstration the airspeed sits 1 knot below the speed you announced for 20 seconds while you explain P-factor. Is that within the CFI standard?
check.a: No. The airspeed tolerance is +5/-0 knots (AI.X.A.S5), so a steady speed below the specified value is outside it; it also moves you toward the stall warning [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

body.p: Ground first. Flight instruction alone on stalls is slower than flight instruction paired with ground discussion of the aerodynamics, and you should review the task before flight even if ground school covered it [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. Slow flight is the same: brief AOA, the backside and the yaw effects before the engine starts.
AC 61-67C gives a stall avoidance plan at slow airspeeds that works as a slow flight syllabus. Fly it with the current standard of no stall warning in mind [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]:

head: AC 61-67C step
What the learner sees
Source
rows: Assigned heading and altitude, slow to just above the stall, trim as needed
The entry and the trim change
Elevator trim at neutral and full nose-up
How trim changes the control pressures
Note the left turning tendency; right rudder to center the ball; release the rudder
Why right rudder grows in slow flight
Turns without rudder pedals
Adverse yaw at low speed
Turns, climbs and descents
Power for altitude, pitch for airspeed
Flap extension and retraction in level flight
Avoiding a stall from flap changes; the change in stall speed
Realistic distractions
Dividing attention while avoiding a stall
Airspeed indicator covered, various flap settings
Flying slow by feel, sound and attitude

body.p: Build the cues on purpose. Each new maneuver is introduced with outside and instrument references together [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], and the learner should learn the feel and sounds of the airplane, such as sensing a nose-high attitude or an out-of-trim condition [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. The covered airspeed indicator drill tests exactly that.

Use slow flight beyond its own lesson. It transfers to short-field landings [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. When a learner struggles with normal landings, a review of the slow flight block lets them do well, regain confidence and build skills for approaches and landings [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

Let the learner find the way out. Safety permitting, let them go part way into a mistake, such as an unnoticed slow speed decay, and recover themselves; a learner who never corrects an error learns the maneuver poorly. If you suspect rote performance, ask for a variation, such as slow flight in the takeoff configuration [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Guard the controls and be ready to take over, especially on a learner's first attempts at a maneuver close to the stall [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Brief the positive exchange of flight controls before the flight [[24:37|AFH 1-16]].

check.q: Your learner covered slow flight aerodynamics in ground school last week. Why still brief it before today's flight?
check.a: Progress through flight instruction alone is slower than when it is paired with ground discussion of the aerodynamics, and the AIH says to review a task with the learner before flight even if ground school covered it [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

body.p: The AFH lists ten common slow flight errors [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. On the checkride the evaluator may fly them as your learner, and you must analyze and correct (AI.X.A.S6). Work out whether each one comes from a misunderstanding or a lack of motor skill; having the learner think aloud makes that easy [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Failure to adequately clear the area [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Power comes back with no clearing turn or callout
Clearing turns with 'clear' called out loud before every maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]]
Inadequate back-elevator pressure as power is reduced [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Altitude drops as the speed decays
Raise the nose to hold altitude as power comes back [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Excessive back-elevator pressure as power is reduced [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
A climb, then a rapid loss of airspeed
Only enough pitch to hold altitude; the speed decay should be gradual [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Insufficient right rudder to compensate for left yaw [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Ball to the right, nose drifting left, worse at high power
More right rudder the closer to the stall and the higher the power [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Fixation on the flight instruments [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Head down, heading wanders, traffic missed
Outside references first, cross-check the instruments [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Failure to anticipate changes in AOA as flaps are extended or retracted [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Altitude or airspeed jump when flaps move
Expect the AOA change; flaps in steps, never abruptly [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Inadequate power management [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Speed keeps decaying or altitude sags in turns
Add power near the target and in turns; pitch for airspeed, power for path [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Inability to adequately divide attention between airplane control and orientation [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Good numbers, but lost position or a missed radio call
Practice with realistic distractions [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a(10)]]
Failure to properly trim the airplane [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Strain on the yoke and altitude wandering
Trim as the speed changes [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Failure to respond to a stall warning [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
The horn sounds and the learner keeps going
React to and correct any stall indication at once [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]

body.p: When the warning sounds, the AC's response is to add power, lower the nose and/or decrease the bank [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. On the checkride, expect the evaluator to make one of these on purpose; name it, say what you saw and give the fix in one sentence (application).

callout.text: Watch the ball and the altimeter from the right seat at the moment power changes. Most of the ten errors show up within a few seconds of a power change: altitude errors, rudder errors and power management errors all start there (application, from the AFH list [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]).

check.q: Your learner's airspeed is right on target but the altitude sags 80 feet in each turn. Which listed error is most likely, and what do you coach?
check.a: Inadequate power management [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]: in slow flight turns it takes more power to hold altitude [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

scenario.title: A slow flight review before first solo on a gusty afternoon
scenario.setup: Your learner has 16 hours and solo is close. Today's plan is slow flight with distractions in a high-wing trainer with a stall horn. The practice area's highest terrain is 1,100 feet MSL. The wind is gusty with light to moderate chop, there is haze, and two other training airplanes use the same area. On the last lesson the learner flew good numbers but kept their eyes on the airspeed indicator.

questions.q: What entry altitude do you plan if the lesson includes a 300-foot descent?
questions.a: 1,100 + 1,500 + 300 = 2,900 feet MSL or higher, so the maneuver ends no lower than 1,500 feet AGL [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] (AI.X.A.S2), with room to recover from an inadvertent stall [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

questions.q: How do the gusts change the margin at the target speed?
questions.a: A vertical gust can raise the AOA suddenly and stall the wing at a higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]], and below L/DMAX a gust that knocks off speed leaves it decaying unless the learner lowers the AOA or adds power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. Consider a slightly higher target today [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

questions.q: The horn chirps once in a gust and the learner corrects at once. Do you count it against them?
questions.a: No. The ACS treats a momentary warning that is recognized and promptly corrected as acceptable (CFI ACS Appendix 3); point out the correction they made: lower the nose and/or add power [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

questions.q: What do you do about the haze and the other airplanes?
questions.a: Haze aggravates collision hazards in practice areas [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Have the learner clear before each turn and maneuver and call 'clear' out loud [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]], remind them the nose-high attitude adds blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]], and share the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: The learner fixes their eyes on the airspeed indicator again. How do you address it?
questions.a: Fixation on the flight instruments and poor division of attention are listed errors [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Use integrated instruction, outside references cross-checked with instruments [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], and try the AC drill with the airspeed indicator covered [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a(11)]].

questions.q: You hand them a chart to find a heading to an airport, and the ball slides right as the airspeed decays in a left turn. What do you want them to do?
questions.a: Fly first: lower the AOA and add power, center the ball with right rudder [[24:116|AFH 5-11]], then return to the chart. Distraction-induced stalls are the real danger [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], and this is exactly the AC distraction drill [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a(10)]].

skills.do: Clear the area before slow flight and before each turn within it, calling 'clear' out loud and explaining the extra blind spots of a nose-high attitude.
skills.practice: Fly every practice session with full callouts as if a learner were copying you [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

skills.do: Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed "no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL)" and explain how you chose it.
skills.practice: Before each flight, write the practice area's highest terrain and your planned descents on the kneeboard and compute the entry altitude [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

skills.do: "Establish and maintain an airspeed at which any further increase in angle of attack, increase in load factor, or reduction in power, would result in a stall warning (e.g., aircraft buffet, stall horn, etc.)", explaining how you found it.
skills.practice: Find the target in each configuration with the AFH method: slow to the warning, lower the nose slightly, add power, note the speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

skills.do: "Accomplish coordinated straight-and-level flight, turns, climbs, and descents with the aircraft configured as specified by the evaluator without a stall warning (e.g., aircraft buffet, stall horn, etc.)" while you explain power, pitch and rudder.
skills.practice: Fly the full sequence in landing, takeoff and clean configurations [[24:116|AFH 5-11]], talking through it out loud each time.

skills.do: "Maintain the specified altitude, ±50 feet; specified heading, ±10°; airspeed, +5/-0 knots; and specified angle of bank, ±5°" while talking.
skills.practice: Have another CFI give you questions to answer while you fly slow flight and call out every deviation you see on the altimeter, airspeed and bank.

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors when the evaluator, acting as a learner, makes them: name the error, say what you saw and give a one-sentence fix.
skills.practice: Fly with another instructor who makes the ten AFH errors on purpose [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]; practice spotting each within a few seconds and correcting it positively [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Under the current AFH and CFI ACS, at what airspeed should the maneuvering part of slow flight be flown?
options: With the stall horn sounding steadily, to show full control at the very edge of the stall
Where any more AOA, load factor or power reduction would bring a warning
At exactly the published 1G stall speed for that configuration
At about 1.3 times the stall speed, the normal approach speed range
quiz.why: The definition: any further increase in AOA or load factor, or reduction in power, results in a stall warning, and slow flight is flown without one [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] (AI.X.A.S3, S4).

quiz.q: AC 61-67C (2000) says to have the student hold heading and altitude with the stall warning device activated. What do you teach today?
options: Follow the AC exactly, since advisory circulars outrank the handbooks
Horn on during training flights, horn off only on the practical test
Hold the speed right at the horn so the learner hears every chirp
Fly just above the warning, and correct promptly whenever it sounds
quiz.why: The AFH and ACS now call for maneuvering without a stall warning and correcting any stall indication [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] (AI.X.A.S4); the AC line is older [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a(2)]].

quiz.q: Which learner statement shows they understand the region of reversed command?
options: Below best endurance speed, flying slower at the same altitude takes more power
Below best endurance speed, cutting the power always makes the airplane fly slower too
Below L/DMAX, the throttle becomes the main control of the indicated airspeed
Near the stall, the elevator works in reverse, so push means the nose goes up
quiz.why: In the region of reversed command a lower airspeed needs a higher power setting to hold altitude; it does not imply that less power gives a lower speed [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]. Below L/DMAX pitch is the better airspeed control [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

quiz.q: Why does an aileron-only turn in slow flight produce more yaw than the same turn in cruise?
options: Torque reaction grows at low airspeed and adds directly to the turn
Gyroscopic precession increases as the forward speed is reduced
Adverse yaw is more pronounced at low speeds, where bigger aileron inputs are used
The ball indicator becomes less accurate at low airspeed and high AOA
quiz.why: Adverse yaw becomes more pronounced at low airspeeds, where larger control inputs are needed [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]], and more aileron deflection means more adverse yaw [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]].

quiz.q: At a high AOA in an airplane whose propeller turns clockwise as seen from the seat, which blade takes the bigger bite?
options: The rising left blade, which shifts the center of thrust to the left
Neither blade, since P-factor only matters during the takeoff roll
The descending right blade, which shifts thrust right and yaws the nose left
The rising blade, which pitches the nose up through gyroscopic precession
quiz.why: At high AOA the downward-moving blade has the higher resultant velocity and more thrust, moving the thrust center right and yawing the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

quiz.q: On your checkride, a gust chirps the stall horn once and you lower the nose slightly and add power at once. How does the CFI ACS treat this?
options: A momentary warning, recognized and promptly corrected, is not unsatisfactory
Any activation of a stall warning device fails the Task on the spot
It is acceptable only if the airspeed also stayed within +5/-0 knots the whole time
You must repeat the whole Task from a new entry altitude and heading
quiz.why: CFI ACS Appendix 3 (Tasks A and B) says a momentary activation from turbulence, recognized and promptly corrected, is not unsatisfactory. A gust can raise the AOA suddenly [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT on the AFH list of common slow flight errors?
options: Fixation on the flight instruments
Failure to properly trim the airplane
Inadequate power management
Flying slow flight in the landing configuration
quiz.why: The landing configuration is how slow flight is typically flown and evaluated [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]; the other three are listed errors [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

quiz.q: Which AIM practice for training flights do you build into every slow flight lesson?
options: Clear the area once at the start, then concentrate on the instruments
Have the learner call out 'clear' left, right, above or below while clearing
Rely on ADS-B In, since it shows every aircraft in a practice area
Clear only before the first turn, because slow flight covers very little ground overall
quiz.why: The AIM urges training operators to have pilots verbalize clearing ('clear' left, right, above or below) and to clear before slow flight [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]; not all aircraft show on ADS-B In [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

quiz.q: AC 61-67C suggests a slow flight drill that hides one instrument. Which one, and with what?
options: The airspeed indicator, at various flap settings and with distractions
The attitude indicator, in clean configuration with the horn disabled
The altimeter, while the learner holds the speed right at the stall horn
The heading indicator, while the learner flies S-turns along a road
quiz.why: The AC says to fly at low airspeeds with the airspeed indicator covered, using various flap settings and distractions [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a(11)]].

quiz.q: A learner is frustrated by poor normal landings. What does the AIH say a return to the slow flight block can do?
options: Replace landing practice entirely until the stage check is complete
Nothing useful, since slow flight belongs only before the first solo
Let the learner do well, regain confidence and build skills for landings
Show the learner that normal landings should be flown right at the stall warning
quiz.why: The AIH example: reviewing the slow flight block lets the learner do well and regain confidence, and builds skills needed for approaches and normal landings [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner found a 55-knot slow flight target flying solo with half fuel. Today, with a heavy passenger and full fuel (still within limits), the horn chirps at 55 knots in the same configuration. What explains it, and what do you coach?
options: Full fuel moves the CG forward, which lowers the stall speed, so the horn must be out of rig; write it up
The POH stall speed is fixed at maximum gross weight, so weight cannot matter; the learner let the nose rise
More weight needs a higher AOA for the same lift, so the stall speed rose; find the target again in flight
A heavier airplane needs less power below L/DMAX, so the learner over-pitched; reduce power and hold 55
final_quiz.why: As weight increases the stall speed increases, because a higher AOA is needed for the extra lift [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100i]]; a forward CG also tends to bring the stalling AOA at a higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]]. Find the target in the configuration flown: slow to the warning, lower the nose slightly, add power to hold altitude and note the speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies slow flight at 57 knots; the 1G stall in this configuration is 50 knots. They roll into a 30 degree level turn using back pressure and no extra power, and the horn sounds. Why?
options: Bank raised the load factor and stall speed, and without added power the speed also decayed toward it
The stall warning vane senses bank angle directly and is set to sound above about 25 degrees
The critical AOA itself becomes smaller in a turn, so the wing reaches it at a lower AOA
The ball moved out of center in the turn, and that sideslip alone triggers the stall horn
final_quiz.why: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]: 50 x square root of (1 / cos 30) = 50 x 1.075 = 53.7 knots. Turns at constant altitude need more power [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]; without it the speed decays [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. The critical AOA does not change [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: During the slow flight entry, before your learner extends flaps and gear, what should they confirm?
options: That the stall horn has already sounded once, to prove the target speed
That the airplane is still trimmed for cruise, so the control pressures stay familiar
That full power is set first, because flaps must never be extended at low power
That the airspeed is within the extension limits, using the before-landing checks
final_quiz.why: Gear and flaps are extended after cruise power is reduced and at appropriate airspeeds so their limits are not exceeded, and the before-landing checks are recommended [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

final_quiz.q: In a descending left turn in slow flight, your learner pushes left rudder to hurry the turn. The ball goes to the right and they feel pushed outward. What is it, and why stop it now?
options: A slip; a stall in a slip rolls the airplane level, so it is a safe way to tighten the turn
A skid; a stall now could start a spin toward the rudder applied, so center the ball first
A skid; skids only matter above maneuvering speed, so at slow flight speed it is just untidy
A slip; the ball always swings outward in descending turns, so no correction is needed now
final_quiz.why: Ball to the outside of the turn with the pilot pressed outward is a skid [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. A stall in a slipping or skidding turn can start a spin in the direction of the rudder applied, regardless of which wingtip is raised, and keeping the nose from yawing is the key to averting it [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: A thunderstorm cell is building next to your practice area while your learner flies slow flight. Why move away and end the drill?
options: Thunderstorms lower the critical AOA of any wing that flies nearby
The stall horn cannot work in the electrical field near thunderstorms
The cell's heavy rain will raise the indicated stall speed by about 10 knots or more
A downburst's wind change can cost lift faster than a slow airplane can recover
final_quiz.why: Downbursts and microbursts are dangerous when the airplane is slow, as in climb and approach; a major wind change can lead to loss of lift and a crash [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner holds altitude within 20 feet but never looks outside and misses a traffic call. Which listed errors fit, and what is the fix?
options: Fixation on the instruments and poor division of attention; outside references cross-checked with instruments
Inadequate power management; set a fixed cruise power and let the airplane find its own altitude
Failure to trim; retrim nose-down so the learner has a lighter yoke and more time to look around
Insufficient right rudder; center the ball first, and the traffic scan will follow on its own
final_quiz.why: Fixation on the flight instruments and inability to divide attention between control and orientation are listed errors [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Integrated instruction uses outside and instrument references together [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: In the covered airspeed indicator drill, your learner holds altitude but the horn sounds. Which cues should have warned them first?
options: The altimeter and the vertical speed indicator, which show slow flight first
The heading indicator, which drifts left in a predictable way as speed decays
Control feel, the sound of the airflow and the pitch attitude of the nose
The outside air temperature, which drops as the airflow over the probe slows
final_quiz.why: Slow flight practice teaches the feel, sound and visual cues of this regime [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]; as speed decreases, control pressures lighten and the sound of the airflow changes [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. The drill is from [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a(11)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner holds slow flight with obvious strain on the yoke, and the altitude wanders ±60 feet. Which error is most likely?
options: Too much rudder trim, which loads the elevator through the interconnected control cables
Failure to trim, so cruise trim leaves strong back pressure and poor control
Fixation on outside references, which hides the altimeter from the learner
Too much power, which pitches the nose up and should be reduced to idle
final_quiz.why: If the airplane stays trimmed for cruise, strong back pressure is needed and precise control is difficult [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]; failure to properly trim is a listed error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

final_quiz.q: The evaluator, acting as your learner, flies slow flight steadily at 54 knots when 55 was specified, with every other value perfect, and asks if they would pass. Your answer?
options: Yes, because the slow flight airspeed tolerance is plus or minus 5 knots
Yes, because 54 knots is inside the private pilot tolerance of +10 knots
Yes, because the CFI ACS accepts any brief deviation as long as it is later corrected
No, because the airspeed tolerance is +5/-0, so steady flight below it fails
final_quiz.why: The standard is airspeed +5/-0 knots (AI.X.A.S5). A steady deviation is not momentary, and flying below the chosen speed moves toward the stall warning [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

final_quiz.q: You want your learner to feel why right rudder matters in slow flight. Which AC 61-67C demonstration fits best?
options: Release the rudder at low airspeed and watch the left yaw, then center the ball
Enter a fully developed spin to the left and recover after one full turn
Pull the mixture to idle cutoff and glide at the slow flight target speed to a landing
Set full left rudder trim, take both feet off and fly a level right turn
final_quiz.why: AC 61-67C has the instructor note the left turning tendency, show that right rudder centers the ball, then release the rudder so the student sees the left yaw [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a(4)]] [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a(5)]] [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a(6)]].

final_quiz.q: A learner says modern trainers are spin resistant, so sloppy rudder in slow flight does not matter. What do you answer?
options: Correct, because a modern trainer cannot be spun at any weight or CG
Wrong: mishandled, uncoordinated slow flight can spin even reluctant airplanes
Correct, but only if the CG is at the aft limit with full flaps extended
Wrong, but only for older airplanes that have no stall horn or stall warning light
final_quiz.why: Modern airplanes are more reluctant to spin, but mishandling the controls in turns, stalls and uncoordinated slow flight can still cause an accidental spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: Why should a learner in nose-high slow flight in a low-wing airplane scan more deliberately than in cruise?
options: Low-wing airplanes have no blind spots below, so only the area above needs care
ADS-B In shows all aircraft in practice areas, so the scan can stay inside
The nose-high attitude adds blind spots, so clear before turns and look often
Slow flight is so slow that other aircraft will see and avoid you first
final_quiz.why: The AIM lists aircraft attitude and wing position as sources of blind spots, notes ADS-B In does not show every aircraft, and calls for clearing before slow flight and turns [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

final_quiz.q: After slow flight in moderate turbulence, your learner asks whether to fly the normal approach speed back at the airport in the same bumps. What does AC 61-67C say?
options: Fly the normal approach speed exactly, since a faster approach only adds float and landing distance
Fly 5 knots slower than normal, since turbulence adds lift to the wing and lowers the stall speed
Fly the slow flight target speed, since the learner has just proven good control at that speed
Carry a higher than normal approach speed, since a gust can stall the wing at a higher airspeed
final_quiz.why: A vertical gust can abruptly raise the AOA, so turbulence can cause a stall at a significantly higher airspeed than in smooth air; in moderate to severe turbulence or strong crosswinds a higher than normal approach speed should be maintained [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

takeaways: Slow flight is flown just above the stall warning, never with it; any warning gets a prompt correction.
The stall comes from exceeding the critical AOA; bank, weight and CG change the speed at which that happens.
Below L/DMAX it takes more power to fly slower; pitch controls airspeed and power controls the path.
Left-turning tendencies and adverse yaw grow at low speed and high power: right rudder and coordinated turns.
Uncoordinated slow flight is a spin setup; keep the ball centered and the nose from yawing.
CFI standard: altitude ±50 feet, heading ±10°, airspeed +5/-0 knots, bank ±5°, finished no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
Teach with ground first, the AC 61-67C low-speed demonstrations and realistic distractions; let the learner find the way out.
cfi_notes: AC 61-67C (dated 9/25/00) paragraph 200a(2) says: 'Have the student maintain heading and altitude with the stall warning device activated' [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a(2)]]. The AFH now sets the target at an airspeed where the airplane is controllable 'without activating the stall warning' [[24:114|AFH 5-9]], and CFI ACS S4 says 'without a stall warning (e.g., aircraft buffet, stall horn, etc.)' (AI.X.A.S4). The checkride uses the ACS, so teach that standard and explain the change if a learner reads the AC.

The CFI ACS objective for this Task says 'maneuvering during slow flight in cruise configuration', while S4 says 'with the aircraft configured as specified by the evaluator' (AI.X.A.S4), and the AFH says slow flight 'is typically performed and evaluated in the landing configuration' [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Be ready for clean, takeoff and landing configurations.

The AFH suggests a target 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall [[24:114|AFH 5-9]], but many warning devices sound 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. The two ranges overlap, so find the real target with the AFH method in each configuration [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

AC 61-67C says a 60 degree level turn raises the stall speed 40 percent [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100b]]; the AFH says 41 percent [[24:114|AFH 5-9]], which matches the square root of 2 (1.414). Use the AFH figure.

For single-engine applicants the evaluator must select Task A or Task B (Demonstration of Flight Characteristics at Various Configurations and Airspeeds) from Area X (CFI ACS Area X note). Prepare both, since they share the slow-speed aerodynamics.

The CFI ACS Appendix 3 note on momentary stall warnings in turbulence applies to you as an evaluator later too: grade continual deviation, lack of correction or lack of recognition, not a single corrected chirp.
From the right seat, the ball and the altimeter right after each power change are the fastest error detectors; most of the ten AFH errors begin there (application from [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]).
Slow flight is a confidence builder as well as a skill: the AIH uses it as the block to revisit when landings go badly [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Plan it into the syllabus more than once.
gaps: None of the sources gives a single target airspeed for slow flight in a given airplane; it depends on configuration, weight and the stall warning, so find it in flight and check the POH/AFM for limits.
The sources do not say how far above the stall warning a learner should fly on a gusty day. That margin is the instructor's judgment, within the ACS +5/-0 knot tolerance on the speed you specify.
The rudder needed, the trim range and the flap and gear extension speeds for slow flight come from the POH/AFM of the airplane you teach in.
The sources do not give a standard script for explaining slow flight from the right seat; the sample here is application built from the AFH procedure.
No source says how many slow flight lessons a learner needs before stalls; that is set by your syllabus and the learner's progress.

activities.title: Slow flight margins in numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You level off at 3,400 feet MSL. The highest terrain in the practice area is 1,250 feet MSL, and the maneuver must end no lower than 1,500 feet AGL. How many feet of slow flight descents can you plan?
items.why: 3,400 - 1,250 - 1,500 = 650 feet [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] (AI.X.A.S2). Plan the descents first, then pick the entry altitude.

items.q: You fly slow flight at 55 knots calibrated airspeed at 8,000 feet. Using the PHAK rule of thumb (add 2 percent to the CAS for each 1,000 feet of altitude), about what true airspeed are you flying?
items.why: 55 x (1 + 0.02 x 8) = 55 x 1.16 = 63.8 knots [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. Altitude has little or no effect on the indicated stall speed; only the true airspeed is higher [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]], so keep the same indicated target even though the ground passes by faster.

items.q: Same airplane, stall 48 knots, flying slow flight at 56 knots. At about what bank angle in a level coordinated turn would the stall speed reach 56 knots?
items.why: Load factor needed = (56 / 48) squared = 1.361. Bank = arccos(1 / 1.361) = 42.7, about 43 degrees [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]] [[24:113|AFH 5-8]].

items.q: Same airplane (stall 48 knots, flying 56 knots), but the horn first sounds at 54 knots wings level, 6 knots before the stall. Stall warning devices alert the pilot as the airplane approaches the critical AOA, so the horn speed rises with the square root of the load factor just as the stall speed does (application). At about what bank in a level coordinated turn does the horn sound?
items.why: Load factor needed = (56 / 54) squared = 1.075. Bank = arccos(1 / 1.075) = 21.6, about 22 degrees [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]] [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:113|AFH 5-8]]. The stall is 43 degrees away, but the warning is only about 22: at this target a 20 degree turn leaves almost no room, and S4 asks for no stall warning.

items.q: The stall speed is 50 knots. Many stall warning devices sound 4 to 8 knots before the stall. What is the highest airspeed at which the horn might first sound?
items.why: 50 + 8 = 58 knots [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. So the AFH's 5 to 10 knot target (55 to 60 knots) [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] might sit right at the horn; find the real target in flight.

activities.title: True or false: power, pitch and the backside
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In the region of reversed command, flying slower at the same altitude takes more power.
cards.why: True. A lower airspeed needs a higher power setting to hold altitude there [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].

cards.s: Below L/DMAX, small pitch changes cause large changes in induced drag and airspeed.
cards.why: True. That is why pitch becomes the more effective airspeed control below L/DMAX [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

cards.s: In level slow flight, part of the thrust acts upward and helps support the airplane.
cards.why: True. A portion of thrust is directed upward in climbs and slow flight and acts as if it were lift [[1:99|PHAK 5-2]].

cards.s: Below L/DMAX, if turbulence knocks off a few knots, the airplane's stability brings the speed back by itself.
cards.why: False. Speed instability means the speed may keep decaying without the pilot reducing the AOA or adding power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

cards.s: On the backside, a little forward pressure can move the airplane toward speeds with excess power to climb or turn.
cards.why: True. The brief descent accelerates the airplane toward the center of the power curve, where there is excess power [[24:91|AFH 4-5]].

cards.s: During level slow flight turns, the power can stay where it was in straight flight.
cards.why: False. During the turns it is necessary to increase power to maintain altitude [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

activities.title: CFI checkride: the evaluator flies as your learner
activities.intro: You are in the right seat. The evaluator plays a 12-hour learner on a slow flight lesson and will make mistakes for you to catch. The practice area terrain tops out at 1,400 feet MSL.

steps.s: The 'learner' levels at 2,700 feet MSL and reaches for the throttle to begin. What do you say?
options: Go ahead; 2,700 feet is plenty for slow flight
Stop: climb so the maneuver ends no lower than 2,900 feet MSL, then clear the area
Descend to 2,000 feet so the ground references are easier to see
Skip the clearing turns, since we cleared on the climb
steps.why: 1,400 + 1,500 = 2,900 feet MSL, so 2,700 is too low before any descent [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] (AI.X.A.S2). Clear before the maneuver [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

steps.s: As power comes back, the altitude drops 70 feet and the 'learner' has not touched the trim. What is the error and the fix?
options: Too much back pressure; push forward to regain speed
Excessive power; pull the throttle to idle
Inadequate back pressure as power is reduced; raise the nose to hold altitude and trim
Fixation outside; look at the attitude indicator only
steps.why: Inadequate back-elevator pressure as power is reduced, resulting in altitude loss, is a listed error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]; raise the nose to hold altitude and trim as the speed changes [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

steps.s: Stabilized, the 'learner' adds power for a climb. The nose yaws left and the ball goes right. What do you say?
options: Right rudder: more power at low speed means more left yaw
Left aileron to stop the yaw
Reduce power; climbs are not part of slow flight
Nothing; the ball always moves in a climb
steps.why: Torque, slipstream and P-factor yaw the nose left at high power and low speed; counter it with right rudder [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Climbs are part of slow flight training [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

steps.s: You hand over a chart as a distraction. The airspeed decays and the horn chirps. What do you expect, and coach if missing?
options: Finish the chart, then fix the speed
Hold altitude with more back pressure
Raise the flaps to gain speed
Fly first: lower the nose slightly and add power, then return to the chart
steps.why: The response to a warning is to add power, lower the nose and/or reduce bank [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]; abrupt flap retraction can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]; the drill teaches dividing attention [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a(10)]].

steps.s: In the debrief the 'learner' asks: 'There was a little frost on the wings this morning. Would that have mattered for slow flight?' Your answer?
options: Light frost only matters at cruise speed, so slow flight practice is unaffected
Even a little frost can raise the stall speed; do not fly until it is all removed
It is fine as long as the stall horn passed its preflight test
Frost matters only for airplanes certified for flight in known icing
steps.why: Even a small accumulation of snow, ice or frost changes the wing's shape and can increase the stall speed, and flight should not be attempted with it on the surfaces [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100k]]. A learner flying at the edge of the warning has no margin for an unknown stall speed (application).
